summary: Specifies the generic structure of the loop that the initiator and acceptor follow to establish a GSS security context. It shows the control flow for both sides, including error handling, and marks where application-specific behavior must be defined.

eli5.summary: Two sides take turns passing messages until they trust each other. This document shows the back-and-forth steps, and what to do when something goes wrong.

questions: what is a gss security context
subtitle: The standard pattern for two parties to establish a secure connection.

tldr.problem: Different applications using GSS-API were writing similar but inconsistent code for the negotiation loop where initiator and acceptor exchange security tokens, with gaps around error handling.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7546 specifies a unified structure for the GSS negotiation loop, covering both the initiator and acceptor perspectives, error conditions, and providing sample C code that applications can reference.
tldr.outcome: Application protocol designers can now point to this RFC instead of specifying their own negotiation logic, reducing duplication and ensuring consistent error handling across different GSS-API users.

today: RFC 7546 is an Informational RFC that provides the authoritative specification for GSS-API negotiation loop structure. It has not been obsoleted and is widely referenced by application protocol standards that use GSS-API.

sections.title: What GSS-API Is and Why This Matters
sections.content:
GSS-API (Generic Security Service Application Program Interface) provides a generic interface for security services that applications can use without worrying about the underlying mechanism. It abstracts over security technologies like Kerberos, NTLM, and others.

When two parties (an initiator and an acceptor) want to establish a secure connection, they exchange messages called tokens in a loop until a security context is established. The GSS-API specification scattered the requirements for this loop throughout multiple places. Different application protocols (SSH, SASL, RPC) had to redefine this loop structure with varying levels of detail and error handling. RFC 7546 consolidates these requirements into one place that other protocols can reference, reducing duplication and improving consistency.
sections.eli5: GSS-API is a security toolkit that lets programs authenticate each other using Kerberos or other methods. Applications were writing the same back-and-forth negotiation code over and over. This RFC shows everyone how to do it the same way.

sections.title: Application Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
Any application protocol using GSS-API needs certain features for the negotiation loop to work correctly. Protocols must provide a way to frame and identify security context negotiation tokens so the application can distinguish them from regular data. Error tokens should also get special framing because the recipient may have no other way to distinguish them.

Protocols may benefit from a generic way to indicate errors with optional descriptive strings, especially when error tokens are not available. If the negotiated security context will be used for per-message operations, protocols need a way to frame and identify those per-message tokens. Additionally, applications are responsible for performing authorization checks on the authenticated peer names returned by GSS-API, since successful negotiation does not automatically grant access to resources.
sections.eli5: Apps need to label the security messages so they know which ones are for negotiation, which are for data, and which are errors. They also need to check if the authenticated user is allowed to do what they asked.

sections.title: The Negotiation Loop Structure
sections.content:
The initiator starts by calling GSS_Init_sec_context() with an empty input token and a fixed set of request flags describing desired properties. The initiator and acceptor then exchange tokens based on the return values (status code and presence of output token). The initiator sends tokens to the acceptor, which processes them with GSS_Accept_sec_context() and sends back response tokens.

The major status codes GSS_S_COMPLETE and GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED determine when to keep looping or stop. If either party receives a token when not expecting one (after context is complete), it indicates a state error. Both parties must perform sanity checks: the acceptor verifies it is expecting a token and handles timeouts if the initiator disappears; the initiator checks that it expects a response before waiting for one. Anonymous initiators must verify the anon_state flag is set before sending tokens to maintain anonymity.
sections.eli5: The initiator goes first with an empty message. The acceptor responds. They keep trading messages until both say the context is complete. If someone gets a message at the wrong time, something is wrong with the other side.

sections.title: After Negotiation and Security Concerns
sections.content:
Once both parties report the security context is complete, the context is not automatically ready for use. Both parties must verify that the returned flags include all required properties. The initiator must check that negotiated flags match what was requested; if a necessary flag is not available, the initiator must destroy the context without using it. The acceptor must similarly verify required flags are set.

GSS-API uses a request-and-check model: requesting a feature does not guarantee the implementation will provide it. Under rare conditions, a context token may arrive after negotiation completes. Such tokens must be processed with GSS_Process_context_token(); at present, these tokens render the context unusable, but future extensions may allow recovery. The security considerations from RFC 2743 and RFC 2744 remain applicable. Implementers should use the GSS_ERROR macro carefully on per-message operations, as misuse has caused security vulnerabilities in existing software.
sections.eli5: After negotiation, both sides must check that they got the security features they asked for. Sometimes late tokens arrive, which must be processed separately. Be careful with error checks to avoid security bugs.

sections.title: Sample Code and Patterns
sections.content:
RFC 7546 provides complete C code using the GSS-API C-bindings showing both initiator and acceptor patterns. The code demonstrates how to set request flags (mutual authentication, confidentiality, integrity), loop until context is established, release buffers properly, and handle errors without leaking resources.

Key patterns shown include: always sending a token if GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED is set or the output token is nonempty; releasing allocated buffers to avoid memory leaks; checking flags after sending a token to catch errors; and performing authorization checks after receiving the initiator's authenticated name. The sample code includes placeholder functions (send_token, receive_token, check_authz) that applications must implement with their own framing and communication mechanisms.
sections.eli5: The RFC provides example code in C showing exactly how to write the negotiation loop for both sides, including when to send and receive messages, how to check for success, and how to clean up.
